<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above -->

#### Description
<!--- Describe your changes in detail -->
- Fix issue where resulting order quantity would place us higher than the target holding percentage
- Refactor logic to streamline process, and hopefully make it easier to read.

#### Related Issue
<!--- This project only accepts pull requests related to open issues -->
<!--- If suggesting a new feature or change, please discuss it in an issue first -->
<!--- If fixing a bug, there should be an issue describing it with steps to reproduce -->
<!--- Please link to the issue here: -->
Closes #5687

#### Motivation and Context
<!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? -->
This bug was a interesting one, basically with the previous implementation it was possible to get values out of `BuyingPowerModel.GetMaximumOrderQuantityForTargetBuyingPower()` that would actually put us over our target holding percentage. This is because once we got our order margin and target margin set we would not consider the total holdings or whether the order was positive/negative for adjustments. (Negative orders would still be rounded down, when really you would want up.)

There was a couple of solutions possible, such as factoring in our quantity holding at the end of the loop and verify that it didn't put us over the margin, then adjust on the next loop. But because of the complexity of the function I worked out a refactor that simplified the process that would not require all values in absolutes, and would always converge on a value that would satisfy our overall margin portfolio target.

For a specific definition of satisfying our portfolio target:
- TargetHoldingsMargin : Amount in dollars the target holdings will cost -> TargetHoldings * UnitMargin 
- TargetMarginAllocated : Amount of portfolio dollars dedicated to this holding -> Target Percentage * (TotalPortfolioValue - RequiredFreeBuyingPower)
✅ TargetHoldingsMargin <= TargetMarginAllocated : Target holdings MUST be less than portfolio target, these values are absolutes so even if we have a short TargetMarginAllocated of -970, we require the TargetHoldingsMargin to be > -970.

It actually reduced the length of the function by ~30 lines and I think its a little more concise because we focus on the end target being the total margin allocated to this asset, which the percentage makes clear. We start by calculating a maximized value for order size that will meet this allocation, and then adjust down accordingly after calculating fees in the `do while` loop. 

I also left in the precaution for an infinite loop where it stops converging and quantity remains the same. This shouldn't happen, but better to be safe. Also there is an addition if the adjustment brings the order quantity to zero, we will immediately return 0 and the reason why.

issue_context.title: GetMaximumOrderQuantityForTargetBuyingPower Calculates Incorrect Quantity for Edge Cases

review_comments: `finalHoldingsQuantity * unitMargin` what about lotSize for the resulting operation?
Not needed for that guy, he is a dollar value for the target holdings margin used if we were to have finalHoldingsQuantity. 😁

These `+1`'s were from the fee ($1) that got changed to 0. 

This was intentionally changed to zero because other tests in the same set, asserted expected results that did not include calculations for a fee. Specifically `VerifyMarginCallOrderLongClosedMarket`, `VerifyMarginCallOrderShortOpenMarket`, `VerifyMarginCallOrderShortClosedMarket`, & `VerifyMarginCallOrderShortOpenMarket`.

To match their expected calculation I removed the fee from the security all these tests share. 👍🏽 

Fee setting is on line 362.
